steps.stem:
The diagonals of rectangle ABCD intersect at E. Given:
\(\begin{cases} CD=3\text{ cm} \\ \angle BEC=120° \end{cases}\)
What is the area of the rectangle (in cm²)?
explanation: The diagonals of a rectangle are equal and bisect each other, therefore \(EB=EC\). Triangle BEC is isosceles, and its base angles are \(\frac{180°-120°}{2}=30°\).
In right triangle BCD, \(\angle DBC=30°\). CD is opposite the \(30°\) angle: it is the short leg, 3. The long leg is \(BC=3\sqrt3\) (the sides are in the ratio \(1 : \sqrt3 : 2\)).
\(S=3\cdot3\sqrt3=9\sqrt3\).

steps.stem: In parallelogram ABCD, the marked parts of angle B are \(3\alpha\) and \(\alpha\), and the marked parts of angle C are \(3\beta\) and \(\beta\). The segments BE and CE meet as in the accompanying figure. What is x?
explanation: Angle B is \(3\alpha+\alpha=4\alpha\), and angle C is \(4\beta\). Adjacent angles of a parallelogram add up to \(180°\): \(4\alpha+4\beta=180°\). Therefore \(\alpha+\beta=45°\).
In triangle BCE: \(x=180°-3\alpha-3\beta=180°-3(\alpha+\beta)=180°-135°=45°\).

steps.stem:
ABCD is a parallelogram, and \(AE\perp BC\). Given:
\(\begin{cases} AD=17\text{ cm} \\ CD=13\text{ cm} \\ EC=12\text{ cm} \end{cases}\)
What is the area of the parallelogram (in cm²)?
explanation: Opposite sides are equal: \(BC=AD=17\) and \(AB=CD=13\).
\(BE=17-12=5\). In right triangle ABE, the sides are \(5, 12, 13\) (a Pythagorean triple). The height is \(AE=12\).
\(S=BC\cdot AE=17\cdot12=204\).

steps.stem:
ABCD is a parallelogram. Given:
\(\begin{cases} AB=10\text{ cm} \\ BC=14\text{ cm} \\ \angle ABC=150° \end{cases}\)
What is the area of the parallelogram (in cm²)?
explanation: The base is \(BC=14\). Drop the height from A. Angle B is obtuse, so the foot H falls on the extension of CB, beyond B.
\(\angle ABH=180°-150°=30°\). In right triangle ABH, the height AH is opposite the \(30°\) angle, so it is half the hypotenuse: \(AH=\frac{10}{2}=5\).
\(S=BC\cdot AH=14\cdot5=70\).

steps.stem: The sum of the lengths of the diagonals of a rhombus is 34 cm. The absolute difference between their lengths is 14 cm. What is its perimeter (in cm)?
explanation:
Call the diagonals \(a>b\). Then:
\(\begin{cases} a+b=34 \\ a-b=14 \end{cases}\)
Add the equations: \(2a=48\). Therefore \(a=24\) and \(b=10\).
The diagonals are perpendicular and bisect each other: the half-diagonals 12 and 5 are the legs of a right triangle. Its hypotenuse, the side, is 13 (\(5, 12, 13\)).

steps.stem:
ABCD is a kite. Given:
\(\begin{cases} AB=AD \\ CB=CD=6\text{ cm} \\ \angle ABD=45° \\ \angle DBC=60° \end{cases}\)
What is the perimeter of the kite (in cm)?
explanation: Triangle BCD: \(CB=CD=6\) and \(\angle DBC=60°\). An isosceles triangle with a \(60°\) angle is equilateral, therefore \(BD=6\).
Triangle ABD: \(AB=AD\), therefore \(\angle ADB=\angle ABD=45°\) and \(\angle A=90°\). It is a 45-45-90 triangle with hypotenuse \(BD=6\).
Each leg: \(AB=AD=\frac{6}{\sqrt2}=3\sqrt2\).

steps.stem: The area of isosceles trapezoid ABCD is 54 cm². DE is an altitude, \(DE=6\) cm, and the area of triangle DEC is 6 cm². What is AD (in cm)?
explanation: Triangle DEC: \(\frac{6\cdot EC}{2}=6\), therefore \(EC=2\).
Drop the height AF too. The trapezoid is isosceles, therefore triangle ABF also has area 6.
The middle rectangle AFED has area \(54-6-6=42\) and height 6: \(AD=\frac{42}{6}=7\).

ABCD is a right trapezoid with \(AD\parallel BC\) and \(\angle ABC=90°\). Given:
\(\begin{cases} AD=9\text{ cm} \\ BC=15\text{ cm} \\ CD=10\text{ cm} \end{cases}\)
What is the area of the trapezoid (in cm²)?
explanation: Drop the height DE to BC. ABED is a rectangle: \(BE=AD=9\), so \(EC=15-9=6\).
Right triangle DEC: hypotenuse 10 and leg 6, so the height is \(DE=8\) (\(6, 8, 10\)).

In trapezoid ABCD, \(AD\parallel BC\). M and N are the midpoints of the legs AB and CD. Given:
\(\begin{cases} MN=11\text{ cm} \\ BC-AD=6\text{ cm} \end{cases}\)
What is the length of BC (in cm)?
explanation: MN is the midsegment, so it is the average of the bases: \(\frac{AD+BC}{2}=11\), and \(AD+BC=22\).
Together with \(BC-AD=6\): add the two equations, \(2BC=28\), so \(BC=14\).

steps.title: Quadrilaterals — area formulas
steps.intro: Pick the formula that matches what the question gives you.

head: Shape
Area
Remember
rows: the height, not the sloping side · angle \(30°\): \(h=\frac12\) side
even if the diagonals do not bisect each other

tips: Trapezoid: drop both heights — a rectangle in the middle, triangles at the ends. Right trapezoid: one height is enough.
Dropped a height? Look for Pythagoras, a triple, or a \(30°\)/\(45°\)/\(60°\) triangle.
Every length \(\times k\) \(\Rightarrow\) area \(\times k^2\) (diagonal \(+50\%\) \(\Rightarrow\) area \(\times2.25\)). Only the base grows? Area \(\times\) the same factor.
Rectangle with the perimeter and the diagonal: \((a+b)^2=a^2+b^2+2ab\) gives \(ab\) — or try a triple.

steps.title: Quadrilaterals — properties
steps.intro: Any quadrilateral: angles add up to \(360°\). Each name adds its own properties.

head: Shape
Sides
Angles
Diagonals
rows: equal · bisect each other · \(\perp\) · bisect the angles — all YES
equal · bisect each other — not necessarily \(\perp\), not necessarily angle bisectors
bisect each other — that's all (not necessarily equal or \(\perp\))
\(\perp\) · bisect each other · bisect the angles — not necessarily equal
two pairs of equal adjacent sides
the main diagonal bisects the angles between the equal sides
exactly one pair of parallel sides (the bases)
the two side triangles have equal areas
base angles equal · opposite angles sum \(180°\)
equal · cut each other into matching pieces

tips: Who is also who: a square is a rectangle AND a rhombus; a rectangle and a rhombus are parallelograms; a rhombus is also a kite. Down the family tree a shape only gains properties.
"Not necessarily": a property of a special shape (a square) is not a property of the general one (a rectangle).
Not sure about a property? Sketch an extreme version — very wide and very low — and look.
Rhombus: symmetric right–left AND top–bottom. Kite: right–left only.
An angle bisector in a parallelogram cuts off an isosceles triangle.
Concave (arrow): the angle in the notch \(=\) the sum of the other three angles.
Midpoints of the sides: of a rectangle — a rhombus; of a square — a square with half the area.
Right trapezoid: always two right angles.

steps.stem: The accompanying figure shows quadrilateral ABCD. Given: angle A is 112° and angle B is 104°. Which of the following cannot be the value of α?
explanation: Call the fourth angle β. The angles of a quadrilateral add up to \(360°\): \(\alpha+\beta=360°-112°-104°=144°\).
Both angles are positive, therefore \(\alpha<144°\). If \(\alpha=144°\), then \(\beta=0°\) — impossible.
The other choices are possible: \(16°+128°\), \(64°+80°\) and \(128°+16°\) all give \(144°\).

ABCD is a concave quadrilateral, as in the accompanying figure. Given:
\(\begin{cases} \angle A=25° \\ \angle B=70° \\ \angle C=35° \end{cases}\)
What is x, the angle ADC marked in the notch?
explanation: The angle in the notch equals the sum of the other three angles: \(x=25°+70°+35°=130°\).
Why: the inside angle at D is \(360°-x\), and the four inside angles add up to \(360°\): \(25°+70°+35°+(360°-x)=360°\). Therefore \(x=130°\).
\(230°\) is the inside angle at D, not the angle in the notch.

ABCD is a parallelogram, and E lies on AD. Given:
\(\begin{cases} AB=7\text{ cm} \\ AE=3\text{ cm} \\ \angle ABC=64° \\ \angle BCE=58° \end{cases}\)
What is the perimeter of the parallelogram (in cm)?
explanation: Opposite angles are equal: \(\angle D=\angle B=64°\). Adjacent angles: \(\angle C=180°-64°=116°\), therefore \(\angle ECD=116°-58°=58°\).
Triangle EDC: \(\angle CED=180°-64°-58°=58°\). Two equal angles, therefore \(ED=CD=AB=7\). (An angle bisector in a parallelogram cuts off an isosceles triangle.)

steps.stem: The diagonals of rectangle ABCD intersect at E. Given: \(BC=12\) cm, and the perimeter of triangle EBC is 25 cm. What is the area of triangle ABE (in cm²)?
explanation: The diagonals of a rectangle are equal and bisect each other: \(EB=EC\). \(EB+EC=25-12=13\), therefore each is \(6.5\) and \(AC=13\).
Right triangle ABC: hypotenuse 13 and leg 12, therefore \(AB=5\) (\(5, 12, 13\)). The rectangle is \(5\cdot12=60\).
The diagonals of any parallelogram (a rectangle too) split it into four triangles of equal area: \(S_{ABE}=\frac{60}{4}=15\).

ABCD is a rhombus. Given:
\(\begin{cases} BD=6\text{ cm} \\ \angle ABD=60° \end{cases}\)
What is the area of the rhombus (in cm²)?
explanation: \(AB=AD\) (all the sides of a rhombus are equal), therefore triangle ABD is isosceles with a \(60°\) angle. It is equilateral: \(AB=AD=BD=6\).
All the sides are 6, therefore triangle BCD is equilateral too.
\(S=2\cdot\frac{6^2\sqrt3}{4}=2\cdot9\sqrt3=18\sqrt3\).

explanation: \(AO=AD=AB\) (the sides of the equilateral triangle and of the square).
\(\angle BAO=90°-60°=30°\). Triangle ABO is isosceles: \(\angle ABO=\frac{180°-30°}{2}=75°\).
\(\angle OBC=90°-75°=15°\). (75° is a trap: it is angle ABO.)

ABCD is a kite, and its diagonals meet at O. Given:
\(\begin{cases} AB=AD=13\text{ cm} \\ CB=CD \\ BO=12\text{ cm} \\ OC=15\text{ cm} \end{cases}\)
What is the area of the kite (in cm²)?
explanation: The main diagonal AC bisects BD: \(OD=BO=12\), therefore \(BD=24\).
Right triangle AOD: hypotenuse 13 and leg 12, therefore \(AO=5\) (\(5, 12, 13\)). \(AC=5+15=20\).
\(S=\frac{AC\cdot BD}{2}=\frac{20\cdot24}{2}=240\).

steps.stem:
ABCD is an isosceles trapezoid with \(AD\parallel BC\). Given:
\(\begin{cases} AB=AD=5\text{ cm} \\ \angle ABD=30° \end{cases}\)
What is its perimeter (in cm)?
explanation: \(AB=AD\), therefore \(\angle ADB=\angle ABD=30°\) and \(\angle A=180°-30°-30°=120°\).
Angles on the same leg add up to \(180°\): \(\angle B=60°\), therefore \(\angle DBC=60°-30°=30°\). The trapezoid is isosceles: \(\angle C=\angle B=60°\).
Triangle BCD has angles \(30°\), \(60°\) and \(90°\). The short leg is \(CD=AB=5\), therefore the hypotenuse is \(BC=2\cdot5=10\).

steps.stem: The perimeter of a rectangle is 11 cm, and one side is 4 cm long. What is its area (in cm²)?
explanation: The other side: \(\frac{11-2\cdot4}{2}=\frac32=1.5\).

steps.stem: In which of the following quadrilaterals are the diagonals not necessarily perpendicular?
explanation: Square, rhombus and kite: the diagonals are always perpendicular.
Rectangle: the diagonals are equal and bisect each other, but they are not necessarily perpendicular. Example: an \(8\times3\) rectangle.

steps.stem: A kite has perpendicular diagonals of lengths 9 cm and 16 cm. A rectangle has the same area and one side of length 12 cm. What is the rectangle’s other side (in cm)?
explanation: The kite: \(S=\frac{9\cdot16}{2}=72\).
The rectangle: \(12\cdot x=72\), therefore \(x=6\).

steps.stem: The diagonals of a parallelogram divide it into four triangles. One of these triangles has area 11 cm². What is the area of the parallelogram (in cm²)?
explanation: The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, therefore they split it into four triangles of equal area.

steps.stem: A square with perimeter 40 cm is divided into 20 congruent rectangles in four rows and five columns. What is the perimeter of each small rectangle (in cm)?
explanation: The side of the square is \(\frac{40}{4}=10\).
Each small rectangle is \(\frac{10}{5}=2\) wide and \(\frac{10}{4}=2.5\) tall.

steps.stem: The midsegment of a trapezoid (the segment that joins the midpoints of its legs) is 9 cm long. One base is 4 cm longer than the other. What is the length of the longer base (in cm)?
explanation: The midsegment is the average of the bases: \(\frac{b+(b+4)}{2}=9\).
\(2b+4=18\), therefore \(b=7\), and the longer base is \(7+4=11\).

steps.stem: The midpoints of the sides of a square with side 10 cm are joined, forming a new quadrilateral. What is the area of the new quadrilateral (in cm²)?
explanation: The new quadrilateral is a square. Its diagonals join the midpoints of opposite sides, therefore each diagonal is 10.
\(S=\frac{10\cdot10}{2}=50\) — half of the big square.
Or: the four corner triangles are \(4\cdot\frac{5\cdot5}{2}=50\), and \(100-50=50\).

steps.stem:
ABCD is a parallelogram. Given:
\(\begin{cases} AB=7\text{ cm} \\ BC=10\text{ cm} \\ \angle ABC=30° \end{cases}\)
What is the area of the parallelogram (in cm²)?
explanation: Drop the height from A to BC. It is opposite the \(30°\) angle in a right triangle with hypotenuse \(AB=7\), therefore it is half of it: \(h=3.5\).
\(S=BC\cdot h=10\cdot3.5=35\).

steps.stem: A parallelogram has base 15 cm and area 90 cm². Its base is increased by 20%, while its height stays the same. What is its new area (in cm²)?
explanation: The height stays the same, therefore the area grows by the same percent as the base.
\(90\cdot1.2=108\). Check: the height is \(\frac{90}{15}=6\), the new base is \(18\), and \(18\cdot6=108\).

steps.stem: The length and the width of a rectangle are each increased by 10%. By what percent does its area increase?
explanation: Every length times \(1.1\) means the area times \(1.1^2=1.21\): an increase of \(21\%\).
Check with numbers: a \(10\times20\) rectangle (area 200) becomes \(11\times22\) (area 242). \(\frac{42}{200}=21\%\).

steps.stem: The diagonal of a square is increased by 50%. By what percent does its area increase?
explanation: Every length times \(k\) means the area times \(k^2\).
The diagonal is multiplied by \(1.5\), therefore the area is multiplied by \(1.5^2=2.25\).
That is an increase of \(2.25-1=1.25\), or \(125\%\). Check: diagonal 2 gives area \(\frac{2^2}{2}=2\); diagonal 3 gives \(\frac{3^2}{2}=4.5\).

steps.stem: A rectangle has area 84 cm². One side is 5 cm longer than the other. What is its perimeter (in cm)?
explanation: Call the sides \(x\) and \(x+5\): \(x(x+5)=84\).
Try factor pairs of 84: \(7\cdot12=84\), and \(12-7=5\). The sides are 7 and 12.

steps.stem: An isosceles trapezoid has bases of 8 cm and 20 cm and legs of 10 cm. What is its area (in cm²)?
explanation: Drop both heights. The difference of the bases, \(20-8=12\), splits into two equal ends of 6.
Each end triangle: hypotenuse 10 and leg 6, therefore the height is 8 (\(6, 8, 10\)).

steps.stem:
ABCD is a right trapezoid with \(AD\parallel BC\) and \(AB\perp BC\). Given:
\(\begin{cases} AD=5\text{ cm} \\ BC=11\text{ cm} \\ AB=8\text{ cm} \end{cases}\)
What is the perimeter of the trapezoid (in cm)?
explanation: Drop the height DE to BC. ABED is a rectangle: \(DE=AB=8\) and \(BE=AD=5\), therefore \(EC=11-5=6\).
Right triangle DEC: legs 6 and 8, therefore \(CD=10\) (\(6, 8, 10\)).

steps.stem: The vertices of the inscribed rhombus are the midpoints of the rectangle’s sides. A half-side of the rectangle is 5 cm and a side of the rhombus is 13 cm, as marked. What is the perimeter of the rectangle (in cm)?
explanation: Each corner triangle is right-angled: hypotenuse 13 and one leg 5. The other leg is 12 (\(5, 12, 13\)).
The rectangle is \(2\cdot5=10\) by \(2\cdot12=24\).

steps.stem: The rectangle consists of 30 congruent unit squares. What is the shaded area?
explanation: Each white kite has perpendicular diagonals 4 and 2: \(S=\frac{4\cdot2}{2}=4\). The two kites: \(8\).
The rectangle is 30, therefore the shaded area is \(30-8=22\).

steps.stem: A rhombus has perimeter 36 cm. Which of the following lengths cannot be the length of its longer diagonal (in cm)?
explanation: Each side is \(\frac{36}{4}=9\).
A diagonal and two sides make a triangle, therefore the diagonal is shorter than \(9+9=18\). 19 is impossible.
The longer diagonal is at least the diagonal of a square with side 9: \(9\sqrt2\approx12.7\). So 13, 15 and 17 are all possible.

steps.stem: Leah says: “Knowing a square’s perimeter is enough to determine its area.” Daniel says: “Knowing a rhombus’s perimeter is enough to determine its area.” Which statement is correct?
choices: Leah is correct and Daniel is incorrect
Daniel is correct and Leah is incorrect
explanation: Square: the perimeter gives the side, and the side gives the area. Leah is correct.
Rhombus: the perimeter gives the side, but the angles can change. A rhombus with side 5 can be a square (area 25) or very flat (area close to 0). Daniel is incorrect.

steps.stem: A congruent isosceles triangle is constructed externally on each side of square ABCD. The square has perimeter 40 cm, and each triangle has perimeter 38 cm. What is the perimeter of the resulting figure (in cm)?
explanation: The four triangles have a total perimeter of \(4\cdot38=152\).
Their bases are the sides of the square, \(40\) in total. They are inside the figure, therefore they are not part of its perimeter.

steps.stem: Which of the following statements is not necessarily true?
explanation: Every rectangle is a parallelogram, every rhombus is a kite, and every square is a rectangle — all three are true.
A parallelogram does not necessarily have perpendicular diagonals. Example: an \(8\times3\) rectangle is a parallelogram, and its diagonals are not perpendicular.

explanation: Drop EF perpendicular to BC. ABFE and EFCD are rectangles.
A diagonal splits a rectangle into two equal triangles: \(S_{EBF}=S_{ABE}=5\) and \(S_{EFC}=S_{ECD}=13\).

steps.title: Symmetry and equal heights
steps.intro: Area questions that look long often fall apart with these facts.

head: Situation
What you know
rows: !A diagonal in any parallelogram (rectangle, rhombus, square)
Two triangles of equal area — each is \(\frac12\)
!Triangle on the full base, tip on the opposite side
Its area is \(\frac12\) of the parallelogram
Several triangles whose bases fill the base (no overlap)
Together they are \(\frac12\) — and white \(=\) shaded
Triangle on \(\frac1n\) of the base, full height
The two side triangles have equal areas ("butterfly")

tips: Shaded-area questions: subtract the white from a shape you know, or break the shaded part into familiar pieces.
Same area does not mean congruent — only same base and same height.

steps.stem:
ABCD is a rectangle. E lies on AD, G lies on BC, and F lies on AB. Given:
\(\begin{cases} AE=2ED \\ BG=2GC \end{cases}\)
Triangles FEG and EGC are shaded. Which of the following additional data is sufficient to determine the total shaded area?
choices: None of these data is sufficient
explanation: E and G split AD and BC in the same ratio, \(2 : 1\). So EG is parallel to AB, and it splits the rectangle into a left part and a right part in the ratio \(2 : 1\).
Let \(S_{ECD}=s\). Then \(S_{EGC}=s\) (a diagonal halves the right rectangle), the right rectangle is \(2s\), and the left rectangle is \(4s\).
FEG stands on the full side EG of the left rectangle, with its tip on AB: \(S_{FEG}=2s\). The shaded area is \(s+2s=3s\), therefore the area of ECD is enough.
The area of AFE or of FBG is not enough: F can be anywhere on AB.

ABCD is an isosceles trapezoid. Given:
\(\begin{cases} AD\parallel BC \\ AD=4\text{ cm} \\ BC=12\text{ cm} \end{cases}\)
The shaded triangle ABD has area 14 cm². What is the area of the trapezoid (in cm²)?
explanation: Triangles ABD and BCD have the same height (the height of the trapezoid). The ratio of their areas equals the ratio of their bases: \(4 : 12=1 : 3\).
\(S_{BCD}=3\cdot14=42\), and the trapezoid is \(14+42=56\).

steps.stem: In quadrilateral ABCD, angle A is α, angle B is 110° and angle C is β. E lies on AB, and DE bisects angle ADC. Which expression equals angle AED?
explanation: Angle sum: \(\angle D=360°-110°-\alpha-\beta=250°-\alpha-\beta\).
DE bisects it: \(\angle ADE=125°-\frac\alpha2-\frac\beta2\).
Triangle AED: \(\angle AED=180°-\alpha-\left(125°-\frac\alpha2-\frac\beta2\right)=55°-\frac\alpha2+\frac\beta2\).
Check with numbers: \(\alpha=100°\) and \(\beta=70°\) give \(\angle D=80°\), \(\angle ADE=40°\) and \(\angle AED=40°\). Only choice 2 gives \(55°-50°+35°=40°\).

explanation: Call the short side of a small rectangle \(x\). Four short sides stack up to one long side, therefore the long side is \(4x\).

steps.stem: A rectangle has a perimeter of 34 cm, and its diagonal is 13 cm long. What is its area (in cm²)?
explanation:
Call the sides \(a\) and \(b\):
\(\begin{cases} a+b=17 \\ a^2+b^2=13^2=169 \end{cases}\)
Faster: 13 suggests the triple \(5, 12, 13\). Sides 5 and 12 give \(P=2(5+12)=34\). It fits, and \(S=5\cdot12=60\).

steps.intro: Perimeter questions with many small pieces usually need only one of these rules.

Perimeter

Rectangular notch cut into a side

tips: Area and perimeter are different questions: \(12\times8\) is an area, \(2(12+8)\) is a perimeter.

steps.stem: A point P lies inside a rectangle. Its perpendicular distances to the left and right sides are 3 cm and 8 cm; its distances to the upper and lower sides are 2 cm and 5 cm. What is the area of the rectangle (in cm²)?
explanation: The width: \(3+8=11\). The height: \(2+5=7\).

steps.stem: A rhombus has area 120 cm² and one diagonal of length 10 cm. What is its perimeter (in cm)?
explanation: \(\frac{10\cdot d}{2}=120\), therefore the other diagonal is \(d=24\).
The half-diagonals 5 and 12 are the legs of a right triangle: the side is 13 (\(5, 12, 13\)).

steps.stem: ABCD is a square. E lies on BC. The shaded triangle AEC has area 30 cm², which is \(\frac3{10}\) of the square’s area. What is BE (in cm)?
explanation: The square: \(\frac{30\cdot10}{3}=100\), therefore its side is 10.
Triangle AEC has height \(AB=10\) to the base EC: \(\frac{10\cdot EC}{2}=30\), therefore \(EC=6\).

steps.stem: An isosceles trapezoid has bases 10 cm and 22 cm and height 8 cm. What is its perimeter (in cm)?
explanation: Drop both heights: the difference of the bases, \(22-10=12\), splits into two ends of 6.
Each leg is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 6 and 8: it is 10 (\(6, 8, 10\)).

steps.stem: ABCD is a rectangle and E lies on AD. Triangle EBC has area 19 cm², and triangle ECD has area 7 cm². What is the shaded area of triangle ABE (in cm²)?
explanation: EBC stands on the full base BC, with its tip on AD. It is half the rectangle.
The two corner triangles make the other half: \(S_{ABE}+S_{ECD}=19\).

steps.stem: A quadrilateral is both a parallelogram and a kite. Its perimeter is 40 cm. Which of the following is necessarily true?
explanation: A parallelogram has equal opposite sides. A kite has two pairs of equal adjacent sides.
Together, all four sides are equal: it is a rhombus. Each side is \(\frac{40}{4}=10\).
The other statements are true only for a square.

steps.stem: ABCD is a concave quadrilateral, as in the accompanying figure. Angles A and C are both α, angle B is 50°, and the angle ADC marked in the notch is 110°. What is α?
explanation: The angle in the notch equals the sum of the other three angles: \(\alpha+50°+\alpha=110°\).
\(2\alpha=60°\), therefore \(\alpha=30°\).

ABCD is an isosceles trapezoid with \(AD\parallel BC\). Given:
\(\begin{cases} AB=9\text{ cm} \\ BC=18\text{ cm} \\ \angle BAC=90° \end{cases}\)
What is α?
explanation: In right triangle ABC, \(BC=18=2\cdot AB\). The hypotenuse is twice a leg, therefore it is a 30-60-90 triangle: \(\angle ACB=30°\) and \(\angle ABC=60°\).
The angles on leg AB add up to \(180°\), and the trapezoid is isosceles: each top angle is \(180°-60°=120°\). \(\alpha=120°\).

ABCD is an isosceles trapezoid with \(AD\parallel BC\). Given:
\(\begin{cases} AB=AD=CD \\ \angle DAC=2t \end{cases}\)
Which expression equals β?
explanation: \(AD=CD\), therefore triangle ADC is isosceles: \(\angle ACD=\angle DAC=2t\).
\(AD\parallel BC\) (Z-angles): \(\angle ACB=\angle DAC=2t\).
\(\angle C=2t+2t=4t\), and the base angles are equal: \(\beta=4t\).

ABCD is a right trapezoid with \(AD\parallel BC\) and \(\angle A=\angle B=90°\). Given:
\(\begin{cases} AD=4\text{ cm} \\ BC=10\text{ cm} \\ \angle C=45° \end{cases}\)
What is the area of the trapezoid (in cm²)?
explanation: Drop the height DE to BC. ABED is a rectangle: \(BE=AD=4\), therefore \(EC=10-4=6\).
Triangle DEC has a right angle and a \(45°\) angle, therefore it is isosceles: \(DE=EC=6\).

steps.stem: The midpoints of the sides of a rectangle with sides 6 cm and 8 cm are joined, forming a quadrilateral. What is the perimeter of this quadrilateral (in cm)?
explanation: The new quadrilateral is a rhombus. Each side is the hypotenuse of a corner triangle with legs \(\frac62=3\) and \(\frac82=4\).
Each side is 5 (\(3, 4, 5\)), therefore \(P=4\cdot5=20\).

steps.stem: ABCD is a rectangle. The two sloping lines meet at C and form an angle of 28°. The two angles marked α are equal. What is α?
explanation: \(AD\parallel BC\): the angle between the shallow line and AD equals the angle between that line and CB at C (Z-angles). That angle at C is α.
The right angle at C is made of α, \(28°\) and α: \(2\alpha+28°=90°\), therefore \(\alpha=31°\).

steps.stem:
ABCD is a parallelogram. Given:
\(\begin{cases} AB=6\text{ cm} \\ BC=10\text{ cm} \\ \angle ABC=60° \end{cases}\)
What is the area of the parallelogram (in cm²)?
explanation: Drop the height from A to BC: a 30-60-90 triangle with hypotenuse \(AB=6\). The leg opposite \(30°\) is 3, and the height, opposite \(60°\), is \(3\sqrt3\).
\(S=10\cdot3\sqrt3=30\sqrt3\).

steps.stem:
ABCD is a square. Isosceles triangles AFB and AED are constructed outside it. Given:
\(\begin{cases} FA=FB \\ EA=ED \\ \angle AFB=2p \\ \angle AED=2q \end{cases}\)
Which expression equals the marked angle FAE?
explanation: Triangle AFB: \(\angle FAB=\frac{180°-2p}{2}=90°-p\). Triangle AED: \(\angle EAD=90°-q\).
The angles around A add up to \(360°\): \(x+(90°-p)+90°+(90°-q)=360°\).

explanation: The height of an equilateral triangle with side 8 is \(\frac{8\sqrt3}{2}=4\sqrt3\). So \(AF=4\sqrt3\).
By symmetry, E is above the middle of AD: \(FE=\frac82=4\).
\(S=\frac{4\cdot4\sqrt3}{2}=8\sqrt3\).

explanation: \(BD=3\sqrt2\) (the diagonal of the square), and it makes a \(45°\) angle with BC.
\(\angle DBF=45°+15°=60°\). BEFD is a rectangle, therefore \(\angle BDF=90°\).

steps.stem: All the rectangles in the accompanying figure are congruent. The shorter side of each rectangle is 2 cm. What is its longer side (in cm)?
explanation: Call the longer side \(L\). The upper row is \(L+2+L\) wide, and the lower row is \(4+L+4\) wide.
\(2L+2=L+8\), therefore \(L=6\).

steps.stem: A rectangle is cut by three mutually parallel segments into four smaller rectangles. Each cut has length 7 cm. The original perimeter is 46 cm. What is the sum of the four smaller perimeters (in cm)?
explanation: Each outer side is counted once in the four small perimeters, and each cut is counted twice.

steps.stem: EF divides rectangle ABCD into two smaller rectangles. The sum of their perimeters is 10 cm greater than the perimeter of ABCD. Given: \(CD=14\) cm. What is the area of the shaded triangle EDC (in cm²)?
explanation: The two small perimeters contain every outer side once and the cut EF twice: \(2\cdot EF=10\), therefore \(EF=5\).
EF is the height from E to CD: \(S=\frac{14\cdot5}{2}=35\).

steps.stem:
ABCD is a rectangle with perimeter 34 cm. E lies on AB, and F lies on CD. Given:
\(\begin{cases} BE=DF \\ EF=7\text{ cm} \end{cases}\)
What is the perimeter of quadrilateral AEFD (in cm)?
explanation: \(BE=DF\), therefore \(AE+FD=AE+EB=AB\).
\(AE+FD+AD=AB+AD=\frac{34}{2}=17\).
Add the cut: \(P=17+7=24\).

steps.stem: The accompanying figure was made by cutting a rectangular notch, 3 cm deep, out of the top side of a 10 cm by 7 cm rectangle. All the angles are right angles. What is the perimeter of the figure (in cm)?
explanation: Push the bottom of the notch back up: the horizontal pieces still cover the width twice, and the outer sides cover the height twice. That is \(2(10+7)=34\).
The two walls of the notch are extra: \(3+3=6\).

explanation: The four squares have a total perimeter of \(4(p+q+r+s)\).
The shared edges (\(r\), \(q\) and \(2p\) in total) are inside the figure, and each was counted twice. Take away \(2(r+q+2p)\).

steps.stem: A square of side length 12 cm has an isosceles right triangle removed from each corner. Each removed triangle has legs of length 2 cm along the square’s sides. What is the perimeter of the remaining octagon (in cm)?
explanation: Each cut takes \(2+2=4\) away from the square's perimeter and adds a hypotenuse of \(2\sqrt2\).
\(P=48-4\cdot4+4\cdot2\sqrt2=32+8\sqrt2\).

steps.stem: In rectangle ABCD, E lies on CD, and \(DE=3EC\). The areas of triangles AED, AEC and ABC are x, y and z, respectively. What is the ratio \(x:y:z\)?
explanation: AED and AEC have the same height from A, and their bases are in the ratio \(DE : EC=3 : 1\). So \(x : y=3 : 1\).
The diagonal AC halves the rectangle: \(z=x+y\).
With \(x=3\) and \(y=1\): \(z=4\). The ratio is \(3 : 1 : 4\).

steps.stem:
ABCD is a trapezoid, and \(a>0\). Given:
\(\begin{cases} AD\parallel BC \\ AD=3a \\ BC=5a \end{cases}\)
E and F lie on BC. The area of trapezoid AEFD equals the combined areas of the two shaded triangles. What is EF?
explanation: The inner trapezoid is half of the whole area, with the same height. So the sum of its bases is half of \(3a+5a=8a\): it is \(4a\).
\(3a+EF=4a\), therefore \(EF=a\).

steps.stem: ABCD is a parallelogram, and AECF is a square. Given: \(AD=12\) cm. The parallelogram’s area is 3 times as much as the square’s area. What is AE (in cm)?
explanation: Call \(AE=x\). It is the side of the square and also the height of the parallelogram to BC, and \(BC=AD=12\).
\(12x=3x^2\). Divide by \(3x\) (it is not 0): \(x=4\).

steps.stem: Two rectangles overlap at an angle of 45°, forming the shaded parallelogram. Their widths are 6 cm and \(4\sqrt2\) cm, as marked. What is the shaded area (in cm²)?
explanation: The tilted side inside the vertical strip is the hypotenuse of a 45-45-90 triangle with leg \(4\sqrt2\). Its length is \(4\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt2=8\).
The height to that side is the width of the tilted rectangle: 6.

steps.stem: A rectangle has perimeter 52 cm and diagonal 20 cm. What is its area (in cm²)?
explanation:
Call the sides \(a\) and \(b\):
\(\begin{cases} a+b=26 \\ a^2+b^2=20^2=400 \end{cases}\)
Use the identity \((a+b)^2=a^2+2ab+b^2\): \(676=400+2ab\), therefore \(2ab=276\).

steps.stem: The diagonals of a convex quadrilateral are perpendicular and have lengths 14 cm and 9 cm. No other side or angle information is given. What is its area (in cm²)?
choices: It cannot be determined from the information given.
explanation: For any quadrilateral with perpendicular diagonals, \(S=\frac{d_1\cdot d_2}{2}\) — even when the diagonals do not bisect each other.

steps.stem: ABCD is a trapezoid with \(AD\parallel BC\). Which of the following data is sufficient to determine its area?
choices: The lengths of its two legs and its height
The length of its midsegment and its height
The lengths of its two diagonals
The lengths of its two bases
explanation: \(S=\frac{AD+BC}{2}\cdot h=\text{midsegment}\cdot h\). The midsegment and the height give the area directly.
The legs and the height do not fix the bases (the whole trapezoid can be wider or narrower). The diagonals alone or the bases alone do not give the height.

steps.stem: In trapezoid ABCD, \(AD\parallel BC\), and the diagonals meet at O. The area of triangle AOD is 4 cm², and the area of triangle BOC is 25 cm². What is the area of the trapezoid (in cm²)?
explanation: The two side triangles have equal areas: \(S_{AOB}=S_{COD}=s\).
AOD and AOB have the same height from A (their bases OD and OB are on BD): \(\frac{s}{4}=\frac{OB}{OD}\). BOC and COD have the same height from C: \(\frac{25}{s}=\frac{OB}{OD}\).
\(\frac s4=\frac{25}{s}\), therefore \(s^2=100\) and \(s=10\).
